newsitem.title: USA: Federal election body impotent to control campaigns.
newsitem.headline: Federal election body impotent to control campaigns.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent
Created over 20 years ago to oversee spending on U.S. political campaigns, the Federal Election Commission now finds itself poorly funded, understaffed and overwhelmed.

The 1996 political campaigns highlighted the problem. Hundreds of millions of dollars were spent on political campaigns by corporations, labour unions and public interest groups, with little or no FEC supervision.

Even when the Commission detects campaign finance irregularities, it has little power to do anything about them. Having no injunctive powersm, the most it can do is seek civil damages in the courts, a process that can be painfully slow.

A bipartisan study on campaign finance reform headed by a number of distinguished political scientists concluded in a report issued this week that the FEC was "poorly and erratically funded, hampering its ability to gather information, disseminate it in a timely fashion and use it to investigate and act on complaints."

"Little if any penalty results from blatant violations of campaign laws. Elections are not overturned ... Candidates and parties willingly take advantage, and never more openly than in 1996," the report said.
The FEC supplied background information and materials for the article, but officials did not want to be quoted. The agency's chairman, John McGarry, was travelling and unavailable for interviews.
The FEC was established in 1975 in the aftermath of the Watergate scandal, which resulted in then-President Richard Nixon being forced to resign.
The body is run by six commissioners -- three Democrats and three Republicans -- nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate to serve six-year terms.
Its job is to monitor the sources and amounts of funds collected by candidates for the presidency and Congress, and to ensure that candidates comply with spending limits.
It also disburses public money to presidential candidates in the form of federal matching funds.

As a vivid illustration of its current woes, one FEC commissioner resigned in 1995 and has not been replaced. The terms of two others also expired that year, although they will continue serving until replacements can be found.
A fourth commissioner's term will expire early next year, by which time it is possible that only two of the six commissioners will be serving their legal terms of office.
The man who resigned, Trevor Potter, said the impotence of the FEC and the difficulty in getting anything done led to his departure.

"The FEC is in no position to regulate the flood of money now flooding through the political system. The body was designed for a world where most people complied with the rules voluntarily, and that's no longer the case," he said.

To add to its woes, public confidence in the FEC seems to be declining. The funds it disburses to candidates come from taxpayers agreeing to set aside three dollars for this purpose when they fill out annual tax returns.

The number of people willing to do so has been falling since 1980 and now stands at only 13 percent of all taxpayers. Meanwhile, Congress has cut the FEC operating budget and last year tried unsuccessfully to force it to fire several staff.
FEC officials say the body has become a convenient whipping boy for both parties.
Earlier this year it took the powerful Christian Coalition to court, arguing that the Coalition was involved in politics, in violation of its tax exempt status.

The Coalition, say FEC officials, declined attempts to mediate the case, preferring a confrontation that could help publicise its cause and serve as a fundraising device. The case may now be in the courts for years.
